uk_market.title: Graduate schemes recruit a year ahead
uk_market.body: Applications usually open between September and December for a start the following autumn. Direct-entry roles are advertised all year and often close within two to three weeks.

uk_market.title: Know the entry routes
uk_market.body: A spring week is a short insight programme, mostly for first and second-year undergraduates. Summer internships and placements often lead to graduate offers. Your university careers service can tell you which ones you are eligible for.

uk_market.title: Check the sponsor register before you apply
uk_market.body: Only employers on the gov.uk register of licensed sponsors can sponsor a Skilled Worker visa. Some employers will hire you on a Graduate visa but cannot sponsor you afterwards.

uk_market.title: UK CVs are two pages
uk_market.body: No photo, date of birth or marital status. Start each bullet with an action and include a number. A cover letter answers why this company before why you.

uk_market.title: Referrals and conversations matter
uk_market.body: Many UK roles are filled through referrals or are never advertised. A 15-minute chat with someone inside a company often does more than several online applications.

where_to_look.name: Graduate and early-career boards
where_to_look.tip: Prospects, Bright Network and Handshake list graduate schemes, internships and entry-level roles with fixed deadlines.

where_to_look.name: Your university careers service
where_to_look.tip: Employers who post here already want graduates from your university, and advisers explain how UK recruitment works.

where_to_look.name: LinkedIn and Indeed
where_to_look.tip: Set daily alerts for your target titles and apply within 48 hours of posting.

where_to_look.name: Company career pages
where_to_look.tip: Roles often appear here first. Check the employers you want every week.

tone_phrases.meaning: Genuinely good. British praise is understated.
Probably will not act on it.

tone_phrases.phrase: We'd love to keep in touch.
tone_phrases.meaning: Usually a polite no. Thank them and do not wait on it.
Often polite and lukewarm, not real enthusiasm.
Neutral. If no date was given, follow up after a week.

tone_phrases.phrase: Do you have any questions for us?
tone_phrases.meaning: Ask two or three thoughtful ones. Saying no reads as low interest.
A 90-second pitch: what you do now, what you did before, why this role.

tone_norms: Confident but understated: 'I led', not 'I single-handedly'.
'We' for team results, 'I' for your exact part.
Expect a little small talk. Ask how their week is going.
Feedback is often indirect. If unsure where you stand, ask one specific follow-up.
Use first names unless told otherwise. 'Sir' and 'Madam' sound overly formal.
cv_rules: Two pages. No photo, date of birth or marital status.
Each bullet starts with an action and carries a number.
Overseas employers get one line of context.
The cover letter answers why them before why you.

phone: Take the call somewhere quiet, with good signal and a charged phone.
Have the advert, the CV you sent and this pack in front of you.
Note the caller's name and thank them by name at the end.
Keep answers to about a minute; long ones lose people.
video: Test the link, camera and microphone 15 minutes before.
Face a window or lamp, with a plain background behind you.
Look at the camera, not the screen, when speaking.
Close other apps and turn off notifications.
Keep the advert and your questions open, but do not read your answers.
in_person: Arrive 10 minutes early. Keep the interviewer's name and number to hand for delays.
Bring a copy of the CV you sent and your questions on paper.
A handshake and first names are normal. Follow the interviewer's lead.
If they check your right to work, they will ask for a share code: get one at gov.uk/prove-right-to-work.

networking_guide.title: From stranger to referral in six steps
networking_guide.intro: Most people will give 15 minutes of advice to someone who asks well. A referral comes later, from someone who knows you a little.
steps: Pick ten people: alumni at companies you like, people in the role you want, and anyone you met at an event.
Connect with a short note: who you are and what you have in common. A free LinkedIn account can add a note to only a few invitations a month, so save notes for the people who matter most.
Once they accept or reply, ask for 15 minutes of advice: not a job, not a referral.
Prepare three questions, keep to time, and end by asking who else you should talk to.
Thank them within 24 hours with one thing you learned. Every month or two, send them something useful.
When a role opens at their company, apply through the advert and ask whether they would be happy to refer you. Make it easy to say no.
networking_guide.note: No reply in two weeks is normal. Send one short follow-up, then move on.

networking_guide.title: Working with recruiters
points: Agency recruiters are paid by the employer. Under UK rules, recruitment agencies cannot charge you a fee for finding or trying to find you work.
An agency may sell extras, such as CV writing or training, but cannot make them a condition of finding you work.
Say what you want, where, and when you can start. If you will need a visa sponsor, ask early which of their clients can sponsor. This is not immigration advice.
Ask them to check with you before sending your CV anywhere, and note where it has gone so no employer gets it twice.
Stay in touch, so they think of you when a role comes in.

networking_guide.title: One UK project, internship or volunteering role
networking_guide.intro: One piece of UK experience, paid or not, gives you something local to talk about and a UK referee.
points: Projects, part-time jobs, internships and volunteering all count. Ask your university careers service first: many run projects with local employers.
Skills-based volunteering puts your studies to work for a charity. Reach Volunteering lists such roles, but asks for three years' professional experience.

On a Student visa, voluntary work is not volunteering: it is a kind of unpaid employment and counts toward your weekly hours. Check with the organisation and your university's international student advisers before you start. This is not immigration advice.
Note what you did and what changed because of it: it becomes an achievement on your profile.

networking_guide.title: Who can give a reference
networking_guide.intro: UK employers often ask for two referees, usually once they have made an offer.
points: Usually one academic referee (a tutor, lecturer or dissertation supervisor) and one from work (a manager or supervisor from a job, placement or volunteering role).
A UK referee helps: an employer can reach them easily and knows how to read what they say.
Friends and family are not referees.
Ask first, say which roles you are applying for, and send them the CV you are using.
Keep in touch with possible referees, so a request never comes as a surprise.
